lesson.title: Judging the Book by Its Cover: The Representativeness Heuristic
lesson.summary: The representativeness heuristic is a mental shortcut in which people judge the probability that something belongs to a category by how closely it resembles their prototype of that category, often while ignoring more statistically important information like base rates.
lesson.body:
A heuristic is a mental shortcut, a rule of thumb that trades some accuracy for speed, letting people reach a judgment quickly without working through every piece of relevant information. The representativeness heuristic is one of the most common of these shortcuts, and it works by judging how likely something is to belong to a category based on how closely it resembles the typical, prototypical member of that category. Instead of gathering statistics or reasoning through probabilities, the mind essentially asks a simpler question: does this look like the kind of thing that belongs in that group? The more closely a description or example matches a mental prototype, the more probable it feels, whether or not that resemblance is actually a reliable guide to real world frequency.

Consider a hypothetical scenario: someone reads a short description of a person named Alex who is quiet, enjoys detailed puzzles, keeps a meticulously organized desk, and has a deep interest in numbers. Asked whether Alex is more likely to be an accountant or a musician, most people say accountant, because the description matches a common stereotype, or prototype, of an accountant far more closely than it matches the prototype of a musician. This judgment feels obviously correct, but it typically overlooks an important fact: the actual probability also depends heavily on how common each occupation is to begin with, information the representativeness heuristic tends to push aside in favor of surface resemblance.

This tendency to overweight resemblance and underweight statistical base rates, how common something actually is in the relevant population, is one of the most well documented consequences of relying on representativeness. Base rate information is dry, abstract, and easy to ignore, while a vivid, specific description that matches a familiar prototype feels immediately compelling. The result is that people often judge probability based almost entirely on how well a case matches a stereotype, even when they have been given the numerical information needed to reach a more accurate answer, because the heuristic operates quickly and automatically, before slower, more deliberate statistical reasoning has a chance to weigh in.

The representativeness heuristic mirrors, in the domain of judgment, the same basic process that schemas and top-down processing use in perception: existing mental categories are used to make sense of new information quickly, by matching new cases against a stored prototype rather than analyzing every case from scratch. This is efficient and often reasonably accurate, since category membership genuinely does correlate with typical features much of the time. But it can also produce real world errors and unfair judgments, including snap assumptions about a person's occupation, personality, or behavior based on superficial resemblance to a stereotype, or a clinician overestimating how likely a patient's symptoms indicate a rare but classic sounding condition while underweighting how much more common a mundane explanation actually is.

The representativeness heuristic is only one of several shortcuts that let people judge quickly instead of calculating precisely, and it is not the only one that can lead reasoning astray. A closely related shortcut skips the question of resemblance entirely and instead judges how likely or frequent something is based on a very different, and equally imperfect, cue: how easily examples of it come to mind, a pattern known as the availability heuristic.
